Title: Real-world PACS integration of automated MRI comparison to improve detection of new or growing multiple sclerosis lesions

Abstract

The detection of new or enlarging T2-weighted lesions is critical for monitoring disease activity in multiple sclerosis. Manual comparison of current and prior MRI scans is time-consuming and prone to inter-radiologist variability. This study evaluates the clinical impact of integrating an automated lesion comparison tool directly into the Picture Archiving and Communication System. We analyzed the detection rates of new lesions in a real-world clinical setting across three hundred patients. Results indicate that automated tools increase the detection of small new lesions while reducing reporting time. The integration demonstrates a significant improvement in diagnostic consistency. We conclude that automated comparison tools enhance the precision of MS monitoring.

Introduction

Multiple sclerosis is characterized by inflammatory demyelinating lesions in the central nervous system. Monitoring the progression of these lesions is essential for assessing treatment efficacy. The current gold standard involves the manual visual comparison of sequential MRI scans by a neuroradiologist. However, this process is subject to human error and cognitive load. Small lesions may be overlooked when comparing scans from different time points. Furthermore, the increasing volume of imaging data puts pressure on clinical workflows. Automated lesion detection and subtraction software have been developed to address these challenges. Most existing research has been conducted in controlled environments using curated datasets. There is a lack of data regarding how these tools perform when integrated into a live clinical PACS. This paper examines the real-world utility of an automated comparison tool. The primary goal is to determine if the tool improves the detection of new or growing lesions. We also assess the impact on the radiologist's efficiency.

Materials and Methods

The study was conducted over a twenty-four month period at a tertiary care center. We included three hundred patients with a confirmed diagnosis of multiple sclerosis. All patients had at least two longitudinal T2-weighted or FLAIR MRI sequences. The automated tool used a deep learning algorithm for lesion segmentation. The software performed rigid registration between the baseline and follow-up scans. It then applied a voxel-wise subtraction analysis to identify new hyperintensities. The tool was integrated into the PACS via a DICOM bridge. This allowed radiologists to toggle between manual views and automated heatmaps. Radiologists first performed a standard manual reading of the current scan. They then accessed the automated comparison overlay to refine their findings. All detected lesions were categorized as stable, new, or enlarging. A senior neuroradiologist acted as the ground truth reference. Discrepancies between the initial reader and the reference were documented. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated for both manual and assisted readings. Time to report was measured from the moment the study was opened.

Results

The automated tool identified a higher number of new lesions compared to manual reading alone. In the manual group, the average number of new lesions detected per patient was one point two. With the assistance of the automated tool, this number increased to one point eight. The sensitivity for detecting lesions smaller than three millimeters increased by fifteen percent. The false positive rate remained low, with most flags being dismissed quickly by the radiologist. There was a notable reduction in the time spent scrolling between historical and current images. The average reporting time decreased by four minutes per case. Inter-observer variability was significantly reduced when using the automated tool. Radiologists reported higher confidence in their assessments of lesion growth. The tool was particularly effective in detecting lesions in the periventricular regions. Some challenges were noted with motion artifacts in the follow-up scans. These artifacts occasionally triggered false positives in the subtraction map. However, the integration into the PACS allowed for rapid verification. The overall diagnostic accuracy improved from eighty-two percent to ninety-one percent.

Discussion

The integration of automated MRI comparison into the PACS workflow addresses a critical gap in MS care. Manual comparison is inherently limited by the resolution of human perception and memory. By highlighting changes in voxel intensity, the tool directs the radiologist's attention to suspicious areas. This reduces the likelihood of missing subtle disease activity. The increase in sensitivity for small lesions is clinically significant. Early detection of new lesions can lead to timely adjustments in disease-modifying therapies. The reduction in reporting time suggests that automation can alleviate clinician burnout. The high specificity observed indicates that the tool does not overwhelm the user with noise. The use of a DICOM bridge ensures that the tool does not disrupt the existing clinical pipeline. We observed that the tool acted as a second reader rather than a replacement. The final decision remained with the clinician, maintaining a human-in-the-loop approach. The impact of motion artifacts suggests that image quality remains a prerequisite for automation. Future iterations of the software could include automated motion correction. The findings suggest that deep learning can be reliably deployed in a production environment.

Conclusion

Automated MRI comparison integrated into PACS significantly improves the detection of new multiple sclerosis lesions. It enhances diagnostic accuracy and reduces the time required for longitudinal analysis. The tool provides a scalable solution for monitoring disease progression in large patient populations. By reducing inter-observer variability, it ensures a more standardized level of care. We recommend the adoption of such tools in neurological imaging centers. Further studies should investigate the long-term impact on patient outcomes. The transition toward AI-assisted radiology is essential for precision medicine in neurology. This study validates the real-world efficacy of automated lesion tracking. The synergy between human expertise and algorithmic precision optimizes the clinical workflow. Ultimately, this leads to better monitoring and management of multiple sclerosis.

The submitted paper investigates whether stochastic gradient descent can cross loss barriers during the optimization of neural networks. This is a fundamental question in deep learning theory as it addresses the ability of SGD to escape local minima. The authors provide a rigorous theoretical framework combined with empirical evidence to support their claims. The mathematical derivations regarding the noise covariance of SGD are sound and well-presented. I appreciate the clarity with which the authors define a loss barrier in high-dimensional spaces. The choice of synthetic landscapes for initial testing is appropriate and allows for a controlled analysis. However, the transition from synthetic examples to real-world architectures needs more elaboration. The paper claims that SGD behaves like a Langevin diffusion process under certain conditions. While this is a standard assumption, the authors should explicitly state the limitations of this analogy. The empirical results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show a clear trend of barrier crossing. However, the sample size of the trials is relatively small and could be increased for better statistical significance. The analysis of the learning rate's impact on crossing probability is particularly insightful. It demonstrates a clear trade-off between convergence speed and the ability to escape suboptimal regions. I suggest adding a comparison with other optimizers like Adam or RMSprop to see if they exhibit similar behavior. The current version focuses exclusively on vanilla SGD, which limits the generalizability of the findings. The figures are generally clear, but Figure 3 is slightly cluttered and requires a larger font for the axes. The related work section is comprehensive and covers the most relevant recent literature on landscape analysis. Some citations from 2024 and 2025 are missing, which would strengthen the current context. The authors should discuss the role of batch size more explicitly as it directly influences the gradient noise. A larger batch size should theoretically make crossing barriers more difficult, but this is not fully explored. The conclusion summarizes the findings well but overstates the universality of the result. Not all landscapes possess the specific barrier structures analyzed in this study. The writing is professional and free of major grammatical errors. The notation is consistent throughout the manuscript, which makes the proofs easier to follow. I recommend that the authors provide the source code in a supplementary repository for reproducibility. This would allow other researchers to verify the observed barrier crossing events. The hypothesis that noise facilitates exploration is well-supported by the data. The distinction between shallow and deep barriers is a strong addition to the theory. The paper makes a meaningful contribution to our understanding of optimization dynamics. I believe the core insights are valuable for the community. With minor revisions to the empirical section, this paper will be a strong addition to the field. I suggest the authors address the batch size query in the discussion section. Overall, the work is high quality and logically structured. I recommend acceptance pending these minor clarifications. The theoretical depth is commendable and the results are provocative. This research helps bridge the gap between stochastic processes and neural network training. The final polish of the figures will enhance the presentation significantly. I look forward to seeing the revised version of this manuscript.

Biological psychology examines how the physical structures and processes of the brain dictate human behavior. The brain influences action through complex networks of neurons that transmit electrical and chemical signals. Neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin regulate mood, motivation, and decision-making processes. Different brain regions specialize in specific tasks, such as the amygdala processing emotion and the prefrontal cortex managing executive function. Historically, this field began with early philosophers debating whether the mind was separate from the body. In the 19th century, phrenology incorrectly suggested that bumps on the skull revealed personality traits. However, the work of Paul Broca and Carl Wernicke proved that specific brain areas control language. The development of the microscope allowed scientists to discover the neuron as the basic unit of the nervous system. Later, the invention of the EEG and MRI enabled researchers to observe the living brain in real time. These technological leaps shifted psychology from purely observational methods to biological evidence. Today, the field integrates genetics and endocrinology to understand how hormones affect behavior. This evolution has led to modern treatments for mental health disorders based on brain chemistry. Understanding this biological foundation is essential for comprehending the human experience.

The paper presents a compelling approach to reducing neural network computational overhead by simultaneously pruning weights and activations. The authors provide a strong theoretical foundation for why joint pruning is superior to traditional weight-only methods. The experimental results demonstrate a significant reduction in FLOPs with minimal loss in accuracy across several benchmark datasets. However, the methodology section lacks a detailed explanation of how the pruning thresholds are dynamically adjusted during training. It would be beneficial to see a more comprehensive comparison against state-of-the-art quantization techniques. Additionally, the paper does not sufficiently discuss the hardware-specific gains, as theoretical sparsity does not always translate to actual speedups. The figures are generally clear, though Figure 3 would benefit from larger axis labels for better readability. The writing is professional and the logical flow of the arguments is easy to follow. I suggest the authors include a complexity analysis of the joint pruning algorithm itself. Addressing the gap between theoretical sparsity and wall-clock time would significantly strengthen the claims. Despite these minor omissions, the research offers a valuable contribution to the field of model compression. I recommend the paper for publication pending the inclusion of the requested clarifications.

This paper proposes a novel homotopy-based stochastic optimization method designed specifically for the training of deep learning models. The authors aim to address the challenge of poor local minima and saddle points by introducing a smoothing parameter that evolves during the optimization process. The theoretical framework is well constructed and provides a rigorous approach to understanding how the objective function transforms. I find the motivation for using homotopy methods in non-convex optimization to be timely and relevant. The introduction clearly outlines the limitations of current stochastic gradient descent variants. It establishes a strong connection between continuation methods and the dynamics of deep neural networks. The mathematical formulation of the homotopy map is precise and easy to follow. The authors successfully define the transition from a simplified convex proxy to the original complex loss landscape. This strategy is conceptually sound and leverages established principles from numerical analysis. The stochastic nature of the updates is handled with care in the derivation. I appreciate the detailed explanation of the noise injection process used to escape sharp minima. The convergence analysis is the strongest part of the manuscript. The proofs are comprehensive and cover several critical scenarios. The authors provide a clear derivation of the convergence rate under specific regularity conditions. I believe the assumption of L-smoothness is standard and acceptable for this type of work. The analysis of the learning rate schedule is particularly insightful. It demonstrates a theoretical bound on the optimality gap that is competitive with existing methods. The transition between the homotopy stages is analyzed with sufficient rigor to ensure stability. However, some of the constants used in the convergence bounds are not fully specified. This makes it difficult to determine the exact practical speed of convergence. I suggest the authors provide a table of these constants for clarity. The empirical evaluation is conducted on a diverse set of benchmarks. The use of MNIST and CIFAR-10 provides a baseline for standard performance. The inclusion of ImageNet results demonstrates the scalability of the proposed method. The results show that the homotopy-based approach consistently reaches lower training losses than Adam and SGD. The generalization error on the test sets is also lower in most cases. This suggests that the smoothing effect helps the model find flatter minima. The ablation studies on the homotopy schedule are useful and informative. They reveal how the decay rate of the smoothing parameter affects the final outcome. The figures are generally clear and well labeled. The plots showing the loss trajectory over time are particularly convincing. I noticed a few typos in the third section regarding index notation. These are minor and do not obscure the meaning of the equations. The discussion section provides a fair comparison with existing continuation methods. The authors acknowledge the increased computational overhead per iteration. This honesty adds credibility to the findings. They argue that the reduction in total iterations compensates for the per-step cost. This argument is supported by the wall-clock time graphs provided in the appendix. I believe the runtime analysis is thorough and honest. The choice of hyperparameters is explained, although a more systematic grid search would be beneficial. It would be interesting to see how the method performs on Transformer architectures. Currently, the focus is primarily on Convolutional Neural Networks. Extending the evaluation to Large Language Models would significantly increase the impact of the paper. The writing style is professional and academic throughout. The flow of ideas from the theoretical setup to the empirical results is logical. The abstract accurately summarizes the contributions of the work. The conclusion ties back to the original goals stated in the introduction. I found the related work section to be comprehensive and well cited. It covers both classical optimization and modern deep learning heuristics. The mathematical notation is consistent across all sections of the paper. The use of lemmas to build toward the main theorem is a good structural choice. I believe the paper makes a significant contribution to the field of stochastic optimization. It bridges the gap between homotopy methods and deep learning practice. The theoretical guarantees provide a necessary foundation for the empirical observations. I am satisfied with the way the authors handled the stochasticity of the gradients. The proof of almost sure convergence is a highlight of the theoretical section. I would like to see more discussion on the sensitivity of the method to the initial smoothing value. Is there a heuristic for choosing this value based on the network architecture? Adding a guideline for practitioners would make the paper more useful. The complexity analysis of the homotopy map computation is efficient. The authors correctly identify that the overhead is linear with respect to the parameter count. This ensures that the method remains viable for very large models. The experimental setup is reproducible, as the authors provided the source code. The clarity of the implementation details is appreciated. I believe the results are statistically significant given the multiple seeds used. The error bars in the accuracy plots are clearly visible. The comparison with second-order methods is a nice touch. It shows that the homotopy method achieves similar benefits without the Hessian cost. This makes it a practical alternative for high-dimensional spaces. The paper is well organized and easy to navigate. The balance between theory and practice is nearly perfect. I believe this work will inspire further research into smoothing techniques for non-convex landscapes. The connection to simulated annealing is hinted at but could be expanded. A brief paragraph comparing the two could add depth to the theoretical discussion. Overall, the manuscript is of high quality and requires only minor revisions. The contributions are clear and the evidence provided is compelling. I recommend the paper for publication after the suggested clarifications are made. The authors should ensure that all symbols in the appendix are defined in the main text. This would improve the readability for a broader audience. The formatting of the references is correct and consistent. The logic used to derive the convergence bounds is flawless. The empirical evidence strongly supports the theoretical claims. I am impressed by the rigor applied to the stochastic analysis. The method shows great promise for improving the robustness of deep learning training. I believe this approach could be extended to reinforcement learning settings. The concept of smoothing the reward landscape is a natural extension. The paper stands as a strong example of principled optimization research. I have no major concerns regarding the validity of the results. The authors have addressed the primary challenges of the homotopy approach. The resulting algorithm is both elegant and effective. I believe the community will find these results very valuable. The integration of homotopy into stochastic frameworks is a non-trivial achievement. The paper is a comprehensive treatment of the subject. It provides a complete roadmap from theory to implementation. I am confident in the findings presented in this research. The clarity of the exposition is a major strength. The authors have successfully communicated a complex idea in an accessible way. I look forward to seeing how this method evolves in future work. The paper is ready for acceptance subject to minor editorial changes. This is a significant step forward for deep learning optimization.

The related works section is thorough, though recent advancements in structured sparsity could be further integrated. The writing is generally clear, although a few technical terms in the methodology section require better definition. Including a complexity analysis of the pruning process itself would also add valuable depth. Overall, this is a strong contribution to the field of model compression. I recommend acceptance pending the clarification of the hardware execution details.

Title: Longitudinal NMR analysis of urinary metabolites to track methylmalonic aciduria, treatment effects, and mutation-related differences

Abstract: Methylmalonic aciduria is a metabolic disorder characterized by the accumulation of methylmalonic acid and other toxic metabolites. This study utilizes longitudinal Nuclear Magnetic Resonance NMR spectroscopy to monitor urinary metabolic profiles in patients over time. We aim to quantify the efficacy of dietary interventions and identify biomarkers associated with specific genetic mutations. Our results demonstrate that NMR can accurately track the fluctuations of methylmalonic acid and related acylcarnitines. We observed a significant reduction in toxic metabolites following strict protein restriction. However, the magnitude of response varied based on the patient genotype. Patients with mutations in the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase gene showed distinct metabolic signatures compared to those with cblA or cblB deficiencies. These findings suggest that NMR is a powerful tool for personalized metabolic monitoring.

Introduction: Methylmalonic aciduria encompasses a group of autosomal recessive disorders that impair the breakdown of branched-chain amino acids. This leads to the buildup of methylmalonic acid in the blood and urine. Chronic accumulation can result in metabolic crises, neurological damage, and renal failure. Current monitoring typically relies on targeted gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. While accurate, these methods are time-consuming and require extensive sample preparation. NMR spectroscopy offers a non-invasive, high-throughput alternative for untargeted metabolomics. Longitudinal analysis allows for the observation of metabolic trends within individual patients. This is critical for adjusting treatment plans in real-time. Understanding how different mutations affect the metabolome is essential for precision medicine. We hypothesize that longitudinal NMR can differentiate treatment responses based on mutation type.

Materials and Methods: We recruited twenty patients with confirmed diagnoses of methylmalonic aciduria. Urine samples were collected every three months over a two-year period. Each sample was stored at negative eighty degrees Celsius until analysis. NMR spectra were acquired using a six hundred megahertz spectrometer with a cryoprobe. Internal standards were added to ensure quantitative accuracy. Spectral preprocessing included phase correction, baseline subtraction, and normalization to creatinine levels. Metabolites were identified by comparing chemical shifts and coupling constants with established databases. Multivariate statistical analysis, including Principal Component Analysis, was used to identify patterns. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to track longitudinal changes. Treatment effects were measured by comparing metabolite levels before and after dietary changes. Genetic mutations were categorized by the specific enzyme or cofactor deficiency.

Results: The primary metabolite identified across all samples was methylmalonic acid. Longitudinal data showed a strong correlation between dietary protein intake and urinary methylmalonic acid levels. NMR successfully detected secondary metabolites such as 3-hydroxypropionate and various methylacylglycines. Treatment with a low-protein diet led to a measurable decrease in these biomarkers within one month. Interestingly, some patients maintained high levels of methylmalonic acid despite strict adherence to diet. These patients predominantly carried mutations in the mutase enzyme itself. In contrast, patients with cofactor deficiencies showed more volatile metabolic profiles. PCA plots revealed clear clustering based on the type of genetic mutation. We observed that certain patients exhibited a higher accumulation of propionylcarnitine regardless of treatment. This suggests a baseline metabolic shift linked to specific genetic variants. The sensitivity of NMR was sufficient to detect subtle shifts in the TCA cycle intermediates. Overall, the metabolic trajectory was highly individualized.

Discussion: Our findings indicate that longitudinal NMR is an effective method for managing methylmalonic aciduria. The ability to quantify multiple metabolites simultaneously provides a holistic view of the patient's metabolic state. The correlation between protein intake and methylmalonic acid confirms the utility of NMR for dietary monitoring. The discovery of mutation-related differences highlights the heterogeneity of the disease. Patients with mutase mutations appear to have a more rigid metabolic phenotype. Those with cofactor defects may be more responsive to specific supplementations. The integration of NMR into clinical practice could reduce the need for invasive sampling. Furthermore, the identification of mutation-specific biomarkers could lead to targeted therapeutic strategies. We must consider the influence of age and weight on urinary metabolite excretion. Future studies should include a larger cohort to validate these biomarker signatures. The use of machine learning could further improve the predictive power of these metabolic profiles.

Conclusion: Longitudinal NMR analysis provides a comprehensive framework for tracking methylmalonic aciduria. It effectively monitors treatment efficacy and reveals critical differences based on genetic mutations. This approach supports the transition toward personalized metabolic healthcare. By quantifying the urinary metabolome, clinicians can optimize dietary interventions for each patient. The study underscores the importance of genotype-phenotype correlations in metabolic disorders. NMR spectroscopy stands as a viable, efficient tool for the long-term management of these complex conditions. Further research will focus on the integration of NMR with other omics technologies. We conclude that metabolic profiling is essential for improving patient outcomes. This methodology can be adapted for other organic acidurias. The results emphasize the necessity of tailored medical care. Overall, this study advances our understanding of methylmalonic aciduria dynamics.

The question of whether students should design their own summer assignments is a subject of significant debate in modern education. Traditionally, teachers assign specific readings or problem sets to prevent learning loss during the long break. However, allowing learners to choose and create their own projects could foster a deeper love for learning. When students have autonomy, they are more likely to engage deeply with the material. This shift moves the focus from mere compliance to genuine curiosity. A student interested in marine biology might spend their summer researching coral reefs rather than reading a generic novel. Such personalized exploration allows learners to connect academic concepts to their own passions. This autonomy encourages the development of critical thinking and self-regulation skills. By setting their own goals, students learn how to manage their time and resources effectively. They must decide what they need to learn and how to prove their mastery of the subject. This process mirrors the independent research required in college and professional careers. Furthermore, student-led assignments can reduce the stress and resentment often associated with summer work. Many students view mandatory packets as a burden that interferes with necessary rest. If the work is self-directed, it feels less like a chore and more like a hobby. Teachers could still provide a general framework or a list of core competencies to ensure academic standards are met. For example, a teacher might require a research project but let the student pick the topic. This balance ensures that learning objectives are achieved while maintaining student agency. Critics argue that students might choose tasks that are too easy or avoid challenging subjects. To prevent this, educators can implement a proposal system where students pitch their ideas for approval. This adds a layer of accountability and ensures the work remains rigorous. The evaluation process could also change from a simple grade to a presentation or a portfolio. Sharing their findings with peers in the fall would create an exciting start to the school year. Ultimately, empowering students to lead their own education promotes lifelong learning habits. It transforms the summer from a period of stagnation into a season of discovery. Transitioning to learner-created assignments acknowledges that every student has a unique path to growth. Education should be about lighting a fire rather than filling a bucket. Therefore, giving students the freedom to shape their summer work is a progressive step toward a more student-centered classroom.

Broccoli rabe, also known as rapini, is a leafy green vegetable belonging to the Brassica family. It is believed to have originated in the Mediterranean region, specifically Italy, where it is a staple of traditional cuisine. Unlike standard broccoli, it features slender stems and small flower buds with a distinctively bitter flavor profile. This bitterness makes it an excellent pairing for rich or salty ingredients. In the kitchen, it is most commonly sautéed with garlic, olive oil, and red pepper flakes. Many chefs recommend adding a splash of lemon juice or vinegar to balance the natural bitterness. It can also be blanched and tossed into pasta dishes or used as a nutrient-dense base for salads. To prepare broccoli rabe, start by trimming the tough, woody ends of the stems. Some cooks prefer to blanch the greens in boiling water for a few minutes before sautéing to mellow the taste. Pat the vegetable dry after washing to ensure it sears properly in the pan. Nutritionally, broccoli rabe is a powerhouse of vitamins A, C, and K. It is an excellent source of antioxidants that help protect cells from damage. The vegetable is also rich in iron and calcium, supporting bone health and blood oxygenation. Additionally, its high fiber content promotes healthy digestion and satiety. Incorporating this green into your diet offers a sophisticated flavor and a boost of essential minerals. Whether served as a side dish or a main component, it is a versatile addition to any healthy menu.

Abstract. This paper examines the stability of a fishery population model integrated with harvesting dynamics through the lens of non-equilibrium thermodynamics. We utilize the concepts of entropy production and dissipative energy to evaluate the system's behavior. The model assumes a logistic growth pattern for the fish population subject to a specific harvesting rate. We derive the entropy production rate based on the flux of biomass and energy transfer within the ecosystem. The dissipative energy is defined as the difference between the energy input and the energy stored in the population. Our analysis shows that the system tends toward a steady state where entropy production is minimized. We investigate the impact of varying harvesting intensities on the stability of the equilibrium points. Results indicate that excessive harvesting leads to a sharp increase in entropy production, signaling instability. The dissipative energy serves as a Lyapunov-like function to prove global asymptotic stability for sustainable harvest levels. We observe that as the population approaches the carrying capacity, the entropy production rate stabilizes. Conversely, overfishing triggers a thermodynamic shift that precedes population collapse. This approach provides a physical basis for determining the maximum sustainable yield. We compare our thermodynamic results with traditional linear stability analysis. The entropy-based method offers a more comprehensive view of the system's robustness against perturbations. We find that the rate of energy dissipation is closely linked to the resilience of the fishery. A high dissipation rate often correlates with a faster recovery from external shocks. However, beyond a critical threshold, dissipation cannot compensate for the loss of biomass. The relationship between entropy and population stability suggests a universal principle for biological resource management. We employ a set of differential equations to describe the population dynamics. The harvesting term is modeled as a proportional function of the current population size. The energy balance equation accounts for metabolic costs and environmental gains. We calculate the thermodynamic force as the gradient of the chemical potential of the biomass. The resulting entropy production is always non-negative, consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. We analyze the phase space of the system to identify attractors. The stability of these attractors is verified using the dissipative energy functional. We demonstrate that the minimum entropy production principle holds for the stable equilibrium. Small fluctuations around the steady state result in a restorative energy flow. We examine the effect of stochastic environmental noise on the entropy production rate. Noise generally increases the average entropy production, reducing the stability margin. We propose a new stability index based on the ratio of entropy production to total energy. This index can serve as an early warning signal for fishery collapse. Our simulations show a clear divergence of the index as the system nears a bifurcation point. We discuss the implications of these findings for policy makers. Managing fisheries based on thermodynamic stability may prevent sudden crashes. We emphasize the importance of maintaining a minimum level of dissipative capacity. The model can be extended to multi-species fisheries by incorporating inter-species competition. In such cases, the total entropy production is the sum of individual species' contributions. We note that biodiversity generally lowers the overall entropy production of the ecosystem. This suggests that monocultures are thermodynamically less stable than diverse populations. We validate our theoretical model using historical data from North Atlantic cod stocks. The data align with the predicted entropy spikes prior to known population declines. We conclude that dissipative energy is a powerful tool for assessing ecological health. The mathematical framework provided here is applicable to other harvested biological systems. We suggest further research into the role of temperature on entropy production in aquatic models. The integration of thermodynamics and ecology bridges the gap between physics and biology. This paper provides a rigorous foundation for energy-based population monitoring. We have shown that stability is not just a mathematical property but a thermodynamic state. The equilibrium of the fishery is characterized by an optimal balance of energy flux. Over-harvesting disrupts this balance, leading to an irreversible increase in entropy. The dissipative energy functional effectively tracks the distance from the stable state. Our results reinforce the necessity of precautionary approaches in fisheries management. We believe that entropy production is a more sensitive indicator than population biomass alone. The study highlights the synergy between non-linear dynamics and thermodynamics. Future models should incorporate the energetic cost of harvesting efforts. We have addressed the primary objective of linking dissipation to stability. The conclusions are supported by both analytical proofs and numerical simulations. This research contributes to the development of sustainable bio-economic models. The use of entropy provides a global perspective on system stability. We thank the academic community for the foundational work on dissipative structures. The findings are summarized in the accompanying data tables. We suggest that the maximum sustainable yield should be adjusted to maintain low entropy production. This ensures the long-term viability of the fish population. The study proves that thermodynamic laws govern the limits of biological exploitation. Our approach avoids the limitations of local stability analysis by using global energy functions. The coherence of the results across different scenarios validates the methodology. We emphasize that ecological stability is intrinsically tied to energy efficiency. The paper concludes that thermodynamic monitoring should be integrated into fishery science. This paradigm shift could lead to more resilient ocean management. The mathematical derivations provided are consistent and reproducible. We have successfully linked the second law of thermodynamics to population ecology. The study demonstrates that stability is achieved when the system optimizes its energy dissipation. Final analysis confirms that entropy production is a reliable proxy for system stress. This completes our assessment of the fishery population-harvesting model.

Indoor air quality is determined by a combination of internal sources, building design, and outdoor environments. Common pollutants include volatile organic compounds from furniture, mold from dampness, and particulate matter from cooking or smoking. Ventilation is a critical factor, as fresh air circulation helps dilute these contaminants and remove stale air. The efficiency of heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems plays a major role in filtering out allergens and regulating humidity. Outside factors, such as smog or pollen, can infiltrate buildings through open windows and gaps in seals. Poor air quality can lead to immediate health effects like headaches, dizziness, and irritation of the eyes and throat. Long-term exposure to indoor pollutants may cause chronic respiratory diseases or aggravate asthma. Occupant behavior, such as the use of chemical cleaners and incense, further impacts the overall health of the space. Maintaining a clean environment through regular filtration and source control is essential for long-term well-being.

The submitted paper presents a compelling approach to enhancing unsupervised visual representation learning to improve performance across image classification, semi-supervised learning, and transfer learning tasks. The authors propose a novel objective function that effectively captures high-level semantic features without requiring labeled data. The methodology is sound, and the experimental setup is rigorous, utilizing standard benchmarks like ImageNet and CIFAR-10. I found the results particularly impressive in the transfer learning section, where the learned features outperformed several existing baselines. The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the contribution of each proposed component to the overall system. However, the theoretical justification for the specific choice of hyperparameters remains somewhat underdeveloped. The authors should provide a more detailed analysis of how these settings impact the stability of the training process. Additionally, the related work section lacks a discussion of recent breakthroughs in masked autoencoders, which are highly relevant to this topic. Comparing the proposed method against these latest architectures would strengthen the paper's claims. There are a few typographical errors in the second section that should be corrected for clarity. The figures are generally well-constructed, although the axis labels in Figure 3 are too small to read. I suggest including a complexity analysis to discuss the computational overhead of the proposed method compared to standard contrastive learning. Despite these minor concerns, the core contribution is significant and offers valuable insights into self-supervised learning. The writing is clear and the logical flow of the arguments is easy to follow. Addressing the mentioned gaps would elevate the quality of the manuscript significantly. I recommend the paper for acceptance pending the requested revisions. Overall, this work represents a meaningful advancement in the field of visual representation learning.

The paper presents an innovative approach to enhancing the few-shot learning capabilities of recurrent neural networks on algorithmic list tasks. By leveraging parametricity, the authors propose a data augmentation strategy that generates logically consistent training pairs based on the structural properties of the functions. The motivation is clear, as RNNs often struggle to generalize the underlying logic of algorithms when provided with limited data. The theoretical grounding in parametricity is strong and provides a rigorous basis for the proposed augmentation method. The experimental setup is comprehensive, covering several standard list-processing benchmarks. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in generalization accuracy compared to standard training baselines. I particularly appreciate the detailed ablation study which isolates the effect of the parametricity-inspired samples. However, the paper would benefit from a more thorough comparison with other common augmentation techniques like noise injection. Some of the notations in the methodology section are overly dense and could be simplified for better readability. The authors should also clarify the computational overhead introduced by the augmentation process during the preprocessing phase. Additionally, it is unclear if this approach generalizes to non-list structured data or more complex recursive functions. The discussion on the relationship between parametricity and inductive bias is insightful but could be expanded. The figures are generally clear, although the axes on Figure 3 require more descriptive labels. The conclusion accurately reflects the findings without overstating the claims. Overall, the contribution is substantial and addresses a critical bottleneck in neural algorithmic reasoning. I recommend acceptance pending the clarification of the mentioned points. This work opens an interesting avenue for integrating type-theoretic principles into deep learning pipelines.

Title: Patient-derived neuroblastoma cultures preserve tumor characteristics and may predict individualized chemotherapy responses

Abstract: Neuroblastoma remains a challenging pediatric malignancy with highly variable responses to standard chemotherapy. This study evaluates the utility of patient-derived primary cell cultures as a tool for precision medicine. We demonstrate that these cultures maintain the genomic and phenotypic traits of the original tumor. Furthermore, ex vivo drug sensitivity assays showed a strong correlation with clinical outcomes. Our findings suggest that patient-derived cultures can predict individualized responses to chemotherapy. This approach provides a viable platform for personalized therapeutic selection.

Introduction: Neuroblastoma is an aggressive neural crest-derived tumor common in infants and children. Treatment strategies typically involve surgery and intensive chemotherapy. However, patient responses vary significantly despite similar histological classifications. The emergence of precision oncology necessitates tools that can predict drug efficacy before clinical administration. Current genomic biomarkers provide some guidance but often fail to capture the functional dynamics of the tumor. Patient-derived models offer a potential bridge between genetic profiling and clinical response. Primary cell cultures are more accessible than patient-derived xenografts for rapid screening. The primary goal of this research was to validate these cultures as predictive models. We hypothesized that primary neuroblastoma cells preserve essential tumor characteristics. We also aimed to correlate ex vivo drug response with in vivo patient outcomes.

Materials and Methods: Tumor tissues were obtained from twenty pediatric patients via surgical resection or biopsy. Samples were processed using enzymatic digestion with collagenase and hyaluronidase. Cells were cultured in specialized media supplemented with growth factors to maintain viability. Phenotypic characterization was performed using immunofluorescence for markers such as PHOX2B and Synaptophysin. Genomic stability was assessed through comparative genomic hybridization and RNA sequencing. For drug testing, cells were exposed to cisplatin, vincristine, and cyclophosphamide. Cell viability was measured using the MTT assay over a seventy-two hour period. The half-maximal inhibitory concentration was calculated for each drug. Clinical data were collected over a twelve-month follow-up period. Response was defined as partial or complete remission according to RECIST criteria. Statistical analysis was performed using Spearman correlation and ROC curve analysis. All procedures were approved by the institutional ethics committee.

Results: All twenty patients yielded viable primary cell cultures. The cultures exhibited a morphology consistent with the original tumor architecture. Immunofluorescence confirmed the presence of neuroblastoma-specific markers in the cultured cells. RNA sequencing revealed a high degree of correlation between the tumor and its culture. Specifically, the expression of MYCN amplification was preserved in all relevant samples. The cultures maintained the differentiation state of the source tumor. Drug sensitivity assays revealed significant heterogeneity among the patients. Some cultures showed high sensitivity to cisplatin, while others were resistant. Vincristine displayed a moderate range of efficacy across the cohort. Cyclophosphamide showed the most variable response patterns. When comparing ex vivo data to clinical outcomes, a significant correlation was observed. Patients whose cultures were sensitive to cisplatin showed higher rates of tumor shrinkage. Conversely, resistant cultures predicted early relapse or disease progression. The area under the ROC curve for cisplatin prediction was 0.82. For vincristine, the predictive value was lower at 0.65. Cyclophosphamide prediction showed a moderate correlation of 0.71. These results indicate that the cultures mirror the pharmacological behavior of the tumor.

Discussion: The preservation of tumor characteristics in vitro is crucial for any predictive model. Our data confirm that primary neuroblastoma cultures retain key genetic and phenotypic signatures. The strong correlation between ex vivo drug response and clinical outcomes is promising. This suggests that these cultures can serve as a functional surrogate for the patient. Traditional genomic markers are static and may not reflect the plasticity of the tumor. In contrast, drug sensitivity assays provide a dynamic measure of therapeutic efficacy. The variability observed in drug responses highlights the need for individualized treatment. Using this platform, clinicians could theoretically avoid ineffective therapies. This would reduce the toxicity associated with unsuccessful chemotherapy regimens. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. Primary cultures lack the complex tumor microenvironment found in vivo. The absence of immune cells and stromal interactions may influence drug response. Additionally, the time required to establish cultures may be too long for some acute cases. Future studies should integrate 3D organoid models to better mimic tissue architecture. Co-culture systems involving immune cells could improve predictive accuracy. The integration of these models into clinical trials is the next necessary step. We believe this approach aligns with the goals of personalized pediatric oncology.

Conclusion: Patient-derived neuroblastoma cultures successfully preserve the characteristics of the original tumor. They provide a reliable method for predicting the efficacy of specific chemotherapy agents. This tool offers a path toward more precise and less toxic treatment strategies. While limitations exist, the predictive power observed justifies further development. The transition toward functional precision medicine may significantly improve survival rates. This study validates the use of primary cultures as a clinical decision-support tool. Further refinement of these models will enhance their utility in pediatric oncology. Personalized chemotherapy selection represents a paradigm shift in neuroblastoma management. Our findings support the implementation of ex vivo screening in clinical practice. Ultimately, this approach aims to deliver the right drug to the right patient at the right time.

Title: Post-Stroke Depression as a Predictor of Recurrent Ischemic Events and Mortality in Observational Cohorts

Abstract
Post-stroke depression is a frequent complication that significantly impairs functional recovery and quality of life. Recent observational evidence suggests that this psychiatric condition is not merely a consequence of brain injury but a potent predictor of adverse clinical outcomes. This paper examines how post-stroke depression correlates with increased rates of recurrent strokes and overall mortality. Through a review of longitudinal data, we analyze the biological and behavioral mechanisms driving these risks. Our findings indicate that patients with depression exhibit higher vulnerability to secondary vascular events. We conclude that screening for depression is critical for secondary stroke prevention.

Introduction
Stroke remains a leading cause of long-term disability and death worldwide. Following the initial event, many survivors experience post-stroke depression, characterized by persistent low mood and anhedonia. While traditionally viewed as a psychological reaction to disability, it is now recognized as a complex neurobiological phenomenon. The relationship between mood disorders and vascular health is bidirectional and synergistic. Observational studies have consistently highlighted a concerning link between depressive symptoms and poor prognosis. Understanding this link is essential for improving long-term patient survival. This paper aims to synthesize evidence regarding depression as a risk factor for recurrence and death. We hypothesize that depression acts through both physiological pathways and lifestyle mediators.

Methods
This analysis is based on a systematic review of prospective observational studies. We selected cohorts with a minimum follow-up period of twelve months. Inclusion criteria required the use of standardized tools, such as the Beck Depression Inventory or the PHQ-9. Data were extracted regarding the incidence of recurrent strokes and all-cause mortality. We focused on studies that adjusted for baseline stroke severity and comorbidities. Statistical models used in these studies typically employed Cox proportional hazards regression. This allowed researchers to calculate hazard ratios for depressive versus non-depressive groups. Diversity in patient demographics across the studies ensured a broad generalizable conclusion. We also examined studies that tracked medication adherence as a mediating variable.

Results
The accumulated data reveal a significant association between depression and recurrent strokes. Patients diagnosed with post-stroke depression show a markedly higher hazard ratio for secondary events. In several large cohorts, the risk of recurrence increased by approximately 50 percent. Mortality rates were similarly elevated among the depressed subgroup. All-cause mortality was higher, regardless of the initial stroke location. The risk remained significant even after adjusting for age and hypertension. Interestingly, the correlation was strongest in the first two years following the index stroke. Patients with severe depression faced the highest risk of early death. Those who recovered from depression showed a subsequent reduction in risk. These results suggest that the timing of depression onset is clinically relevant.

Discussion
The mechanisms linking depression to recurrent stroke are multifaceted. From a biological perspective, depression is associated with systemic inflammation. Increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines can promote atherosclerosis and plaque instability. Furthermore, depression often correlates with dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. This leads to chronic cortisol elevation and impaired glucose metabolism. Such physiological changes create a pro-thrombotic state in the vascular system. Behavioral factors also play a decisive role in this relationship. Depressed patients often exhibit lower adherence to antihypertensive and antiplatelet medications. They are more likely to engage in sedentary behavior and poor dietary habits. Smoking cessation rates are typically lower in patients suffering from depression. These lifestyle factors compound the biological risks, creating a dangerous cycle. Social isolation further exacerbates the poor prognosis by reducing support systems. The lack of motivation for physical rehabilitation also hinders cardiovascular health. Consequently, the synergy of biological and behavioral factors elevates the risk of mortality.

Clinical Implications
These findings necessitate a shift in the standard of post-stroke care. Mental health screening should be integrated into the primary neurological follow-up. Early identification of depression allows for timely pharmacological and psychological intervention. Antidepressants, particularly SSRIs, may provide both mood stabilization and potential neuroprotective effects. Cognitive behavioral therapy has shown efficacy in reducing depressive symptoms and improving adherence. Integrating psychiatric care into stroke units can reduce the burden of recurrent events. Clinicians must view depression as a modifiable risk factor for vascular health. Family involvement in the recovery process can mitigate the effects of social isolation. Comprehensive care plans should prioritize both physical and mental rehabilitation. This holistic approach is likely to lower overall mortality rates.

Conclusion
Post-stroke depression is a powerful predictor of recurrent strokes and mortality in observational settings. The evidence suggests that depression increases vulnerability through inflammatory pathways and poor health behaviors. The strong correlation observed across various cohorts underscores the urgency of mental health integration. Reducing the prevalence of depression can potentially decrease the incidence of secondary vascular events. Further research is needed to determine if treating depression directly reduces the risk of recurrence. However, current observational data provide a compelling argument for proactive screening. Addressing the psychological aftermath of a stroke is as critical as managing blood pressure. By treating the mind, we can better protect the brain. Future guidelines should mandate depression screening for all stroke survivors. This strategy will ultimately improve survival rates and functional independence.

Title: Systemically delivered rhenium-188 liposomes for glioma treatment: efficacy, survival, and radiation safety in rats

Abstract
Glioblastoma multiforme remains one of the most lethal malignancies due to its invasive nature and the restrictive blood-brain barrier. This study investigates the therapeutic potential of rhenium-188 labeled liposomes administered systemically to treat glioma in rat models. Re-188 is a beta-emitting isotope capable of delivering targeted radiotherapy. We evaluated the efficacy of these liposomes in reducing tumor volume, increasing overall survival, and ensuring radiation safety for healthy organs. Results indicate that liposomal delivery enhances the accumulation of Re-188 within the tumor site. Significant tumor regression was observed in the treatment group compared to the control. Survival rates were markedly improved, although some toxicity was noted in the kidneys. These findings suggest that Re-188 liposomes are a promising candidate for targeted glioma therapy.

Introduction
The treatment of high-grade gliomas is complicated by the heterogeneity of the tumor and the difficulty of drug delivery to the brain. Traditional surgery and external beam radiation often fail to eradicate infiltrating cells. Systemic delivery of radiopharmaceuticals offers a way to target dispersed tumor cells. Rhenium-188 is an attractive isotope because it provides both high-energy beta particles for therapy and gamma emissions for imaging. However, free Re-188 has poor pharmacokinetic properties and lacks specificity. Liposomes serve as effective nanocarriers to encapsulate radioactive isotopes, protecting them from rapid clearance. They can be modified to cross the blood-brain barrier and target glioma cells specifically. The goal of this study was to assess whether Re-188 liposomes could effectively treat gliomas when delivered intravenously. We hypothesized that liposomal encapsulation would increase the residence time of the isotope in the brain. Furthermore, we aimed to determine the safety profile regarding off-target radiation.

Materials and Methods
Male Sprague-Dawley rats were used for this experimental study. Glioma cells were implanted orthotopically into the right striatum of the rats to simulate human glioblastoma. The animals were randomly divided into three groups: a control group receiving saline, a group receiving free Re-188, and a group receiving Re-188 liposomes. Liposomes were prepared using the thin-film hydration method with DPPC and cholesterol. Rhenium-188 was incorporated into the liposomal bilayer through a specialized chelating process. The average diameter of the liposomes was measured using dynamic light scattering. The systemic dose of Re-188 was standardized across the treatment groups. Intravenous injections were administered via the tail vein. Tumor growth was monitored using magnetic resonance imaging at weekly intervals. Survival was recorded as the time from implantation to natural death or euthanasia. Biodistribution was assessed by gamma counting of organs at various time points. Radiation safety was evaluated by examining histological sections of the liver, kidneys, and lungs.

Results
The MRI scans revealed a significant reduction in tumor volume for the Re-188 liposome group. In contrast, the free Re-188 group showed only minimal inhibition of tumor growth. The control group exhibited rapid tumor progression with significant edema. Liposomal delivery resulted in a higher concentration of the isotope within the tumor mass. The half-life of the isotope in the brain was extended by five-fold when encapsulated in liposomes. Survival analysis showed that the median survival of the liposome group was 42 days. The free Re-188 group survived for a median of 28 days, while the control group survived for 18 days. Statistical analysis confirmed a p-value of less than 0.01 for survival differences. Gamma scanning indicated that the majority of the radioactive dose accumulated in the liver and spleen. However, the concentration in the brain was sufficient to induce necrosis in the tumor core. Histological analysis of the brain showed extensive apoptosis in glioma cells. There was minimal radiation damage to the surrounding healthy brain parenchyma. The kidneys showed signs of mild tubular necrosis in the free Re-188 group. Liposomal delivery reduced the renal toxicity compared to the free isotope. The liver showed some inflammation, which is common with nanocarrier delivery. No significant pulmonary toxicity was observed in any of the groups.

Discussion
The results demonstrate that Re-188 liposomes effectively penetrate the blood-brain barrier to reach glioma cells. The use of liposomes prevents the rapid excretion of the isotope through the kidneys. This allows for a prolonged exposure of the tumor to beta radiation. The beta particles from Re-188 have a short path length, which minimizes damage to distant healthy tissues. This localization is critical for treating brain tumors where precision is paramount. The increased survival rate proves that systemic delivery can be a viable alternative to local injections. We observed that the liposomes likely utilized the enhanced permeability and retention effect. This effect is common in malignant tumors with leaky vasculature. The reduction in renal toxicity suggests that liposomes shield the kidneys from direct isotope exposure. However, the accumulation in the liver remains a concern for long-term safety. Future studies should focus on ligand-based targeting to further refine delivery. Attaching peptides that target the transferrin receptor could increase brain uptake. This would allow for lower systemic doses and reduced liver toxicity. The combination of Re-188 with chemotherapy might yield synergistic effects. Our data supports the transition to larger animal models for further validation. The imaging capability of Re-188 allows for real-time dosimetry. This enables clinicians to adjust doses based on individual patient responses.

Conclusion
Systemically delivered Re-188 liposomes provide a significant therapeutic advantage over free radiopharmaceuticals in the treatment of glioma. The efficacy is evidenced by decreased tumor volume and increased survival rates in rats. Radiation safety is improved in the kidneys, though liver uptake remains a factor to be optimized. This approach represents a potent strategy for targeted radiotherapy in the brain. Further optimization of the liposomal surface will likely enhance the therapeutic index. We conclude that Re-188 liposomes are a promising tool for the clinical management of glioblastoma.

References
1. Smith J, et al. Radiopharmaceuticals in Neuro-oncology. Journal of Nuclear Medicine, 2020.
2. Lee K, et al. Liposomal Delivery Systems for Brain Tumors. Nanomedicine, 2021.
3. Wang H, et al. Rhenium-188 Properties and Applications. Radiation Research, 2019.
4. Brown M, et al. Blood-Brain Barrier Challenges in Glioma Therapy. Cancer Cell, 2022.
5. Garcia L, et al. Beta-emitting Isotopes for Targeted Therapy. Nuclear Medicine Biology, 2018.

Title: Social and Demographic Influences on Rift Valley Fever Awareness and Prevention among Nomadic Herders in Nigeria

Abstract
Rift Valley fever is a zoonotic disease that poses significant threats to animal health and human livelihoods in sub Saharan Africa. Nomadic herders in Nigeria are particularly vulnerable due to their close contact with livestock and movement across diverse ecological zones. This study examines how social and demographic factors influence the awareness and preventive practices regarding the virus. Data were collected from five hundred herders across northern Nigeria using structured questionnaires. Results indicate that education levels and age significantly correlate with knowledge of disease transmission. Furthermore, social networks and community leadership play a critical role in the dissemination of preventive information. The findings suggest that targeted public health interventions are necessary to bridge the awareness gap.

Introduction
Rift Valley fever is caused by a Phlebovirus and is primarily transmitted through the bites of infected mosquitoes. It can also be transmitted to humans through direct contact with infected animal blood or tissues. In Nigeria, the disease manifests as sporadic outbreaks often linked to heavy rainfall and flooding. Nomadic herders constitute a vital part of the agricultural economy but remain underserved by formal healthcare systems. Their mobile lifestyle complicates the delivery of veterinary services and health education. Understanding the barriers to awareness is essential for controlling the spread of the virus. Previous research has focused on clinical outcomes, yet social determinants of health are often overlooked. This paper aims to analyze how specific demographic variables shape the perception of risk among these populations. By identifying these influences, policymakers can develop more effective communication strategies.

Materials and Methods
The study employed a cross sectional descriptive design conducted between January and June 2026. The target population consisted of nomadic herders residing in the Sahel and Sudan savanna regions of Nigeria. A multi stage sampling technique was used to select participants from various migratory routes. The sample size of five hundred individuals ensured a representative distribution across different age groups and ethnicities. Data were collected using a pre tested questionnaire administered in local languages including Fulfulde and Hausa. The questionnaire was divided into three sections covering demographics, awareness levels, and prevention practices. Awareness was measured based on the ability to identify symptoms and transmission routes. Prevention practices included vaccination of livestock and the use of insect repellents. Statistical analysis was performed using chi square tests to determine associations between variables. The study adhered to ethical guidelines, ensuring informed consent and confidentiality for all participants.

Results
The demographic profile of the participants revealed a predominance of males aged between thirty and fifty years. Education levels were generally low, with over sixty percent of respondents having no formal schooling. Regarding awareness, only thirty five percent of the herders could correctly identify Rift Valley fever. Those with primary education were twice as likely to recognize the disease as those without any schooling. Age played a nuanced role, as older herders relied more on traditional knowledge than official health warnings. Socioeconomic status showed a positive correlation with the adoption of preventive measures. Herders with larger herds were more likely to have sought veterinary advice during previous outbreaks. However, the use of mosquito nets and repellents remained low across all demographic groups. Social influence was strongest among those belonging to organized herder associations. These associations served as primary hubs for information sharing regarding livestock health. Gender analysis indicated that women in nomadic camps had even lower awareness levels than men. The lack of access to radio or mobile phones was a significant barrier to receiving timely alerts.

Discussion
The results demonstrate a clear link between formal education and disease awareness. Education provides the cognitive tools necessary to understand complex zoonotic cycles. The low awareness rates suggest that current government outreach programs are not reaching the nomadic population. The influence of age indicates a generational divide in how health information is trusted. Older herders often view official interventions with skepticism, preferring ancestral methods of animal husbandry. This highlight the need for community based approaches that integrate traditional leadership. The role of herder associations proves that peer to peer communication is more effective than top down mandates. When a trusted community leader advocates for vaccination, adoption rates increase significantly. The gender disparity in awareness suggests that women are excluded from health discourses despite their role in processing animal products. This exclusion creates a blind spot in the prevention chain, as women often handle raw milk and meat. The limited use of insect repellents can be attributed to both cost and a lack of perceived risk. Many herders view mosquito bites as a trivial part of their environment rather than a vector for disease. The correlation between herd size and veterinary contact suggests that economic investment drives health seeking behavior. This implies that poor herders are at a higher risk of both infection and economic loss.

Conclusion
Social and demographic factors profoundly influence the awareness and prevention of Rift Valley fever among Nigerian nomadic herders. Education, age, and social connectivity are the primary drivers of knowledge acquisition. There is a critical need for tailored health communication that accounts for the mobile nature of the population. Integrating veterinary services with human health outreach, known as the One Health approach, is essential. Public health campaigns should utilize local languages and traditional communication channels. Empowering community leaders and herder associations can accelerate the adoption of preventive measures. Special attention must be paid to including women in health education programs. Improving access to mobile technology could provide a real time warning system for outbreaks. Government funding should be directed toward mobile clinics that follow migratory routes. Reducing the cost of livestock vaccines would encourage broader uptake among low income herders. Future research should explore the psychological barriers to risk perception in these communities. Ultimately, a multidisciplinary strategy is required to mitigate the impact of Rift Valley fever. Such an approach will protect both human health and the livestock economy of Nigeria. Strengthening the resilience of nomadic populations is key to regional health security. Through inclusive and culturally sensitive interventions, the burden of this disease can be reduced. This study provides a baseline for implementing these necessary changes. Effective prevention depends on bridging the gap between scientific knowledge and community practice. Continuous monitoring and evaluation of these strategies will ensure long term success. Collaboration between the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture is paramount. Only then can Nigeria achieve a sustainable reduction in zoonotic disease prevalence.

The paper presents an interesting approach to mitigating optimization-induced learning failure through an epoch-delayed regularization strategy. The authors clearly define the problem of early-stage instability and provide a logical motivation for delaying regularization. The proposed method is easy to implement and does not introduce significant computational overhead. The theoretical justification for why this delay prevents premature convergence to poor local minima is well-reasoned. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate a consistent improvement in final accuracy and training stability. However, the paper would benefit from a more comprehensive ablation study regarding the optimal length of the delay period. It is currently unclear if the chosen delay is universal or highly dependent on the specific network architecture. Additionally, a comparison with other warm-up strategies, such as learning rate ramping, would strengthen the claims of novelty. The writing is generally clear, though some mathematical notations in the methodology section are slightly ambiguous. A few figures would benefit from larger axis labels for better readability. The related work section is thorough, covering most relevant literature on regularization and optimization. Despite these minor concerns, the core contribution is sound and provides practical value to the community. The proposed strategy offers a simple yet effective tool for training deep neural networks. I recommend the paper for publication provided the authors address the requested clarifications.

This paper presents a compelling approach to stabilizing Generative Adversarial Network training by utilizing Cramer distance and energy-based discriminators. The authors successfully demonstrate that these modifications help mitigate the common issue of mode collapse, providing more stable gradient flow during optimization. The theoretical grounding is solid, and the mathematical derivation of the energy-based loss is clear. However, the experimental section would benefit from a broader range of datasets to further validate the generalizability of the method. While the quantitative results are promising, more qualitative comparisons with current state-of-the-art models are needed. The ablation study effectively highlights the contribution of each component, but the computational overhead of the new discriminator is not fully discussed. I suggest the authors include a detailed analysis of training time and memory usage. Despite these minor omissions, the work offers a significant contribution to the field of generative modeling. I recommend acceptance pending the inclusion of these additional evaluations.

Students learn to manage their time more effectively when their day is structured around various learning modules. By prioritizing comprehensive support within the school walls, the educational system can foster a more holistic approach to development. Ultimately, extending the school day transforms the learning experience from a race against the clock into a journey of discovery. This approach ensures that students are not only academically proficient but also emotionally balanced and well-rested.
